extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and composing poems (especially Romantic/lyric poetry) with attention to unity of style, diction, imagery, character-choice, and the relation of moral intent to poetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconstancy of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sudden and unprepared transitions from lines or sentences of peculiar felicity to a style that is unimpassioned or undistinguished; do not alternate abruptly between the ‘poetic’ style, the prose-only style, and the neutral/common style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should prepare the reader for heightened language rather than surprising them with sharp shifts which produce anticlimax or hyperclimax. Coleridge compares the awkwardness to the jarring insertion of songs in comic opera and praises Metastasio’s practice of placing the aria at the end of a scene and raising the recitative immediately preceding it. Anti-patterns: sequences where a passage of striking originality is immediately followed by plain, prosaic lines (examples cited from THE BLIND HIGHLAND BOY and other passages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid laborious minuteness in pictorial description
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from excessive, painstaking fidelity in the representation of objects and their positions—verse should not read like a draughtsman’s catalogue or force the reader to construct a diagram line by line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve detailed, literal description only for cases where it is necessary to the intelligibility of the tale. Prefer ‘creation’ — presenting a whole picture flashed at once — to tedious, piecewise painting. Example positive model: Milton’s 'fig-tree' passage that presents the whole co-presence of the image. Anti-pattern: long descriptive stretches (cited pp. 96–98 of THE EXCURSION) that cause the reader effort rather than imaginative immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid insertion of accidental or superfluous circumstances/biographical minutiae
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overload a poem with incidental facts or the biographical minutiae of characters when such particulars are unnecessary to the poem’s operation; such accidental detail can contravene the essence of poetry (the ‘most catholic and abstract’ art) and distract the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical episodes and detailed episodes belong more properly to history or novels meant to pass for history (Defoe-style). In poetry, characters should remain representative; unnecessary specifics divide the reader’s faith and may render fiction false rather than fictitious. Anti-pattern examples: pedlar/Leech-gatherer backstories in THE EXCURSION that add little to poetic effect and require explanatory episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of characters should serve poetic aims (representative rather than biographical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose characters whose social rank or particularities are motivated by the poem’s aim; avoid particularizing rank where nothing follows that the rank explains or illustrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the poet’s object is to awaken general human feeling, he should work with representative figures rather than detailed life-histories. If a lowly character is chosen, its selection must be justifiable within the poem’s design; otherwise the reader is distracted by the attempt to reconcile improbable particulars with the poet’s claims. Horace’s precepts on characterization are invoked: avoid details that perplex rather than support the poetic fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow dramatic form to produce ventriloquism or stylistic incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dramatic form cautiously: either the dramatised utterance will be stylistically unlike the poet’s own diction (producing incongruity), or it will be indistinguishable from the poet’s voice (producing ventriloquism where two speak but one speaks really).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing in dramatic guise, create distinct, believable voices; ensure that speech-forms fit speakers without betraying the poet’s personal diction unless intended. Failure produces odd stylistic shifts or the impression that a single authorial mind is pretending at multiple speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intensity of feeling disproportionate to knowledge or occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let intensity of feeling outrun the knowledge of, or appropriate relation to, the objects described; excessive passion may yield prolixity, repetition, and an eddying rather than progressive thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain proportion between feeling and circumstance so general readers can sympathize. Examples of the anti-pattern: passages in which feeling loops and repeats instead of advancing (cited pages/lines in the Poems and THE EXCURSION). Keep progression clear and avoid unnecessary amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid thoughts and images too great for the subject (mental bombast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steer clear of a disproportion of thought to circumstance—grandiose thoughts or exalted images that the occasion does not warrant (a form of ‘mental bombast’ rather than mere verbal inflation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fault is most often the province of genius misapplied: magnificent conceptions that should be reined in to match the simplicity or scale of the subject. Examples: sublime metaphors applied to trivial or domestic images (e.g., sudden fall from 'inward eye' to 'dances with the daffodils') and overblown apostrophes to children whose attributes become absurd or unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match register and imagery to the subject (avoid abrupt burlesque shifts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the level of image and diction appropriate across adjacent lines and stanzas; avoid sinking abruptly from elevated, profound lines to trivial, everyday ones so that the effect becomes burlesque or jarring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that lofty lines are supported by their context and that lighter concluding lines do not degrade preceding grandeur. Example: the couplet 'They flash upon that inward eye... / And then my heart with pleasure fills, / And dances with the daffodils' is cited as an abrupt and potentially burlesque descent in register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clarity and sensibility in paradox and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that paradoxes and lofty metaphors convey intelligible meaning; do not assert grand attributes (e.g., calling a six-year-old a 'Mighty Prophet' or saying a child is 'for ever haunted' by the Eternal Mind) unless their sense can be coherently supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If words are taken in common sense they must not convey absurdity; if reinterpreted against common usage to avoid absurdity, they must not become mere banalities. Metaphor/paradox must either be defensible within the poem’s logic or avoided as unintelligible or trivializing.

rubrics_metrics.name: The poet’s primary object should be to communicate pleasure (moralizing comes after)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ought to proceed upon the 'state of association which actually exists as general' and to minister pleasure first; moral truth should follow via the pleasure produced, not be presented as the poem’s immediate and primary object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to make poetry an immediate vehicle of moral or philosophical argument (truth as immediate object) risks destroying the distinction between poetry and prose/philosophy and perplexes the reader. Use delight as the introducer to any moralizing effect; avoid turning the poem into a sermon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve appropriateness and purity of diction (austere purity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for an austere purity of language, grammatically and logically — perfect appropriateness of words to meaning and preservation of diction from affectation and misappropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge values 'untranslatableness' (an ideal test: the diction cannot be translated into ordinary words of the same language without injury to meaning) and includes in 'meaning' the associations words recall. Maintain precision, luminous distinction, and self-possession in phrasing. Avoid the ‘vicious phraseology’ common in sermons, newspapers, and popular speech; cultivate logic and verbal exactness from early education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use language to create co-presence (paint to the imagination, not to the fancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor creative words that create the co-presence of the whole picture immediately (creation) over descriptive listing that appeals merely to fancy and requires the reader to reassemble parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ devices that excite vision by sound and use cross-sensory associations (the 'vestigia communia of the senses') so the image is complete to the imagination at once. Model passages: Milton’s camera-obscura style; avoid scattered or dissected map-like description.
